8 optical engines/GPU introduces 100x more lasers than scale out switching. More conservative estimates were 10x laser content from AOI's CFO.

From what I've seen yearly capacity expansion for lasers generally increase around ~3x Y/Y like $AVGO projections, or ~5x over 2-3 years like Furukawa's. 

This is what I mean by optical content like lasers + requirements (more InP substrates), rises per generation and bottlenecks on UHP ranges might persist through 2030 despite aggregate capex decreasing.

Which is what I'm trying to argue here. 

Future CPO laser competitors like Furukawa/AOI/Shija are more nuanced, since AOI is focused on 800G/1.6T transceivers (which faced capacity expansion delays + DSP Bottlenecks), but they have capability for 400mW+ ranges + ongoing CPO qualifications. 

I don't think transceivers have the same durability though in capex reduction scenarios, which is why I've been arguing the valuable optionality AOI has to focus on merchant lasers is mispriced. 

A lot of it is execution/qualification rather than demand, $LITE + $COHR are the most de-risked with confirmed long term visibility. 

But entire AI trade is moving up and down together.

Well, most of the time projections are noise and reactionary. 

Like right now, sky-high projections for $ANT $700-$800B ARR over next few years is stirring up hype that I'd argue gets revised down later. 

I do think it's important to model in capex forecasts dropping past 2028, due to the current reflexive nature of AI selloffs, rate hikes, etc. 

The drawn out duration of Iran War doesn't help, Jensen leaving $NVDA certainty draws concerns over Nvidia's ecosystem. 

But any catalyst, like if Iran War ends, can also change sentiment in a heartbeat (since bearish positioning is overwhelming). 

- It's also clear financing has been tightening, since OpenAI only managed to raise $11B of their original $30B target so far. 

- Markets are reacting enthusiastically to companies like $TE doing a $100M ATM today (nuking valuations)

- Although the "guppy" sector is probably the most sensitive to financing + rate changes.

On bright side... Neoclouds like $NBIS or $IREN  seem to be adjusting by getting 100% capex prepayments or 90% GPU prepayments from their counterparties. 

What I'd argue though is lower aggregate capex does not apply uniformly in supply chains.

- Mid-high range lasers for NPO/CPO are still sold out, as seen with $LITE now starting negotiations for 2030 capacity.  
- MLCCs are seeing further tightening as content usage goes up for AI servers
- ABF substrates to InP substrates not really going anywhere. 

If content per system goes up 10X-15X, capacity expands at 2-3X Y/Y, and capex drops 28%. 

And content is so cheap that you can triple order and screw over competitors with wafer supply... 

I'm pretty confident you'll see acceleration upstream in bottlenecks from optical components to substrates despite potential aggregate capex dropping. 

Another rant is: 

-I keep seeing this argument that "low P/E is a warning for cyclical that's going to crash" but these are just clown takes

Nobody seems to analyze duration scenarios like capacity expansion vs. content changes vs. demand. to actually see how long those earnings last. 

If everyone seems to be exiting DDR2 lines, there's probably going be more tightness in 2027 despite consume demand weakening, even if it looks like it's low P/E. 

- Also for concerns about CPO "delays", the same components like lasers are used for NPO. You'll still see 150-200mW NPO lasers or ELS NPO using the same 300–400+ mW lasers as CPO. 

We'll just see acceleration with NPO as a bridge if CPO gets delayed and higher range lasers likely to remain in a severe shortage. 

- Feels like markets have also completely discredited the merit of take/pay price floor LTAs as well that companies like SK Hynix to Samsung have.

If contractual agreements hold up, memory players look very undervalued.  

TLDR:
- I think it's important to model in capex decreasing to numbers like -30% in hypothetical downside sceanrios. 

Given AI profitability, it's clearly not sustainable for hyperscalers to aggregately increase capex $500B or $1T+ Y/Y, and that's never been a case I've argued. 

- This is also not the same thing as demand destruction that markets are overreacting to now (which haven't happened yet). 

- We can see demand revisions for GPUs, ASICs, and heavier cost parts of the supply chain, while acceleration increases elsewhere.  

The nuances market miss by indiscriminately selling everything is going to present compelling opportunities when the dust settles. I think in the end institutions are probably going to end up owning more of the same names retail discovered early on. 

Anyway, I think it's a good idea to try and survive until more earnings comes out.

Re: The new BIS rule

I missed a provision yesterday.

Under the new rule, chip designers in China and other restricted regions can no longer qualify for an exemption through the existing transistor-count verification process unless they have BIS status as an “approved” or “authorized” IC designer. Under the previous rule, a foundry or an outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) provider could verify the transistor count to establish eligibility for an exemption. Now, BIS itself has to decide whether to grant one.

As a result, foundries such as TSMC and Samsung Electronics, as well as OSAT providers such as ASE and Amkor, will need to conduct more thorough background checks on their customers.

$MRVL has lost about 50% of its value in one month. 

Today CEO Matt Murphy emailed every employee to explain it, under the subject line "Putting the Week in Perspective."

What happened, in his words:

1. Last week Marvell agreed to combine with $LITE. Murphy says "some of the initial analyst commentary and media coverage reflected a misunderstanding of the strategic rationale."

2. The large shareholders he met in Boston and New York "told a very different story." He says they understood the case for joining silicon and optics, and recognized Marvell's acquisition track record.

3. Their most common question was "why now?" His answer points to Inphi, which put Marvell ahead of the move to scale-out optics. Optics are now moving into scale-up and scale-in, and "customers are making important technology decisions now that will shape the next generation of AI infrastructure."

4. On the stock, he gives the number plainly. "Marvell shares declined approximately 51%, closely in line with the 49% average decline among our connectivity peers." $LITE saw a similar decline.

5. He ties that to a selloff across AI stocks. Part of the cause is "uncertainty about how long the current AI infrastructure investment cycle will continue." He adds that the midterms "brought increased attention" to data center expansion and "the possibility of additional restrictions."

6. His counterpoint is the longer window. "Marvell shares are still up approximately 66% year to date," ahead of both connectivity and broader AI peers, and he says the long-term trends behind AI infrastructure spending "remain strong."

7. He ends by telling staff the deal alone won't pay off. "Simply acquiring a company doesn't create value. It's what we do afterward." That part is still far off, because the deal isn't expected to close until the first half of 2028 and the two companies stay independent until then.

Everyone’s acting like Jensen leaving Nvidia is the end of the world. And look, I’m bummed about it too, and not just because of my portfolio. But Nvidia fell about 30% from its October 29 close to Thursday’s low, like the company just stops existing without him.

Steve Jobs resigned on August 24, 2011, and even though the market didn’t take much of a hit, the mood around Apple was somber.

When Tim Cook took over, people said he was just an operator and that no one could replace Steve. There’s some truth to that, yet Tim ran Apple at the speed of light.

Fifteen years later, the stock was up 23.6x (28x with dividends), and Apple went from a $350B company to over $4T.

Nvidia just handed the keys to its CFO for now, until they find the perfect fit. And no, it won’t be the same, and sometimes that’s for the best.

These are thrilling times we’re living in.

$SPCX $ANT $RKLB $ASTS $NBIS

Last time a $1T+ company went public, $RKLB and $ASTS got crushed.

SpaceX listed on June 12. Over the next 47 days, $QQQ fell 8%, while $RKLB fell 43% and $ASTS 36%, more than 4x the market. From their pre-IPO peaks, both were down about 60%.

People owned them as a way into SpaceX. The moment they could buy the real thing, they dumped them. I mean, why wouldn't they? Just remember that SpaceX itself had a massive drawdown after its inflated IPO.

Bitcoin got hit first, down 26% into the roadshow while the Nasdaq barely moved.

Semis bottomed during the roadshow, ran 17% into the week after the listing, then fell 25% into the bottom. That bottom came 47 days after the first trade, and from there everything bounced.

Now it's Anthropic's turn.

It launched its roadshow on November 10 and is reported to start trading on November 19, the exact same 9-day gap as SpaceX. Day 47 lands in early January.

Bitcoin is already down 25% from its October high. Last time it was down 23% at this exact point.

The difference is semis. 

At this point before SpaceX listed, they were 6% off their high. Today they’re 23% off. A big chunk of the selling has already happened.

So who gets hit this time?

Anything people bought as a way into Anthropic: $SKM, which owns a stake, and the high-beta AI names.

Just because it happened before doesn’t mean it has to happen again. But there’s a consensus that Anthropic is sucking the living air out of high-beta AI names, and to an extent the hyperscalers too. 

It won’t last forever, and we’re due for a rebound.

This time won’t play out exactly the same, but it’s worth keeping this timeline in mind.

英伟达今晚这份财报，数字已经不重要了

北京时间明早 5:20 出数，6:00 电话会。

共识营收 1,091 亿、EPS 2.47 美元。季报的数字其实早就落袋了——过去四个季度它都超自己指引中点 4.6% 到 5.7%，这次大概率还是超。

所以今晚唯一还算数的数字，是四季度指引：市场要 1,250 亿。给不到，就是问题。

但真正的定价权在「话」上。念数字的人换了：临时 CEO Colette Kress，干了 13 年 CFO，董事会还在挑正式人选。

而这场电话会上最有杀伤力的一句话，三个月前就是她自己说的。8 月 26 日她给了 FY2028 营收增长约 70% 的展望，当场定性为「受供给约束」——当时华尔街只预期 44%。今晚她敢不敢原样再说一遍，就是全部。

三个看点。

一，四季度毛利率。她自己说过底部在 71%–72%，市场现在只给 70.2%。底部要是往下挪，整条 AI 硬件链一起重估。

二，内存。8 月她把毛利率下滑归因于「内存极端定价」，而下游定价在涨、上游成本也在涨。重点不是成本多高，是她能不能把成本转出去。

"NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA) today announced that the Board of Directors has established the National Security and Export Control Oversight Committee, a new standing committee responsible for board-level oversight of the company’s national security policies, export control compliance and global trade risk management. It will meet at least quarterly, including with management and in executive session. The Committee will oversee the Company’s ongoing efforts to enhance its internal National Security Team and Global Trade Compliance Team, and work closely with independent third-party experts in law, national security and global trade compliance.

“NVIDIA recognizes that advanced silicon technologies and the emergence of artificial and superintelligence present unprecedented challenges for national security.
